text: This is Talk to your Company. A live 3D twin of your plants that you can talk to, built for a single NVIDIA Jetson Thor.

A plant manager with several buildings and floors cannot watch every camera. Near misses, people in restricted zones and missing helmets go unseen. And a simple question means walking there, or calling someone.
So we built a twin you can ask. Speak a question. The twin flies to the right floor, shows what the cameras see, and answers out loud.
Two plants, six floors, six cameras. Every person and vehicle the cameras see becomes a live marker on the right floor.
Select a plant and its floors spread apart. Conveyors, racks, machines and restricted zones all come from one configuration file.
Ask in plain language, by voice or by text. Give me a status of both plants, and you get people, vehicles and open events.
Say, show me plant two, floor three, and the camera flies there while the assistant answers.
Ask about safety, and the events of the last ten minutes light up on the twin.
And when a question is out of scope, it says so, instead of guessing.
Focus a floor to see its live camera, with every detection boxed.
Here, a worker has stepped into a restricted zone. The alert names them.

Ask, who is this person? You get the name, role and shift, when they entered, how long they stayed, and that they were not authorised. Follow-up questions work too. The people are fictional, and identity comes from a simulated badge feed, not from face recognition.
One more sentence writes the incident report. It is filled from the event record, so it cannot contain invented facts.
For a live demo, drop any recording, or your webcam, into a floor's camera, and it is analysed on the spot.

Under the hood, there are two pipelines. First, perception. Video is decoded, a YOLO detector finds people and vehicles, a tracker follows them, and a homography maps pixels to floor metres. Rules turn those tracks into four kinds of safety event, stored on the device.
Second, the voice path. Whisper transcribes the question, a vision language model chooses a tool, and Piper speaks the answer, sentence by sentence.

All of it is built to run live on one NVIDIA Jetson Thor. The detector is exported to Tensor R T and batches all six streams. One vision language model handles both reasoning and vision, so everything fits inside fifteen gigabytes of memory. And one command starts it, fully offline.
On screen, a heads-up display shows frames per second, voice latency, GPU and memory. And the promise that matters: no audio or video leaves the device.
Every heavy component also has a mock, so the same code runs on a laptop without a GPU. That is how this recording was made.
Talk to your Company. Ask your plant a question.
